Stadium Stories: Stadio Olimpico

19th October 2026
Share
  • facebook
  • x
  • Link copiedcopy-link

Rising beneath the slopes of Monte Mario in the heart of Rome, the Stadio Olimpico is a stadium shaped by a magnificent sporting heritage.

0:00 / 5:05
Instaread

Home to Italian rugby's biggest occasions, it is a venue where Guinness Men's Six Nations drama unfolds against a backdrop unlike any other in Europe.

Part of the vast Foro Italico sporting complex, the stadium has welcomed Olympic champions, World Cup finalists and generations of passionate supporters. Today, with more than 70,000 seats, it remains the seat of Italian rugby and one of the most iconic arenas in world sport.

Built for a changing Italy

The story of the Stadio Olimpico stretches back long before its official opening.

Construction of the wider complex began in 1928, with architects envisioning a vast sporting centre on the north-western edge of Rome. Progress was interrupted by the Second World War, and the stadium would not be fully completed until 1953, when Italy hosted Hungary in the first match at the new venue.

Originally known as the Stadio dei Centomila, or "Stadium of the 100,000", it reflected the ambition of a nation keen to establish itself on the international sporting stage. Over the decades, renovations transformed the ground from a huge concrete bowl into the modern arena seen today.

For many Italians, the stadium's evolution mirrors that of Rome itself: ancient foundations continually adapted for a new era.

The arena of rivals

Few major stadiums in Europe serve two fierce rivals simultaneously.

The Stadio Olimpico is shared by AS Roma and SS Lazio, whose Derby della Capitale remains one of football's most intense occasions. Throughout the season, the Curva Sud is draped in the colours of Roma while the Curva Nord belongs to Lazio's most passionate supporters.

  • 2027 Guinness Men's Six Nations fixtures

On rugby weekends, however, the divisions disappear. Azzurri supporters from across Italy replace club loyalties with national pride, transforming the stadium into a sea of blue as they gather behind Gonzalo Quesada's side.

Locals often joke that the Olimpico is the only place in Rome where rival fans can briefly agree on something.

Olympic heritage

The clue is in the name.

Ahead of the Rome 1960 Olympic Games, the stadium underwent a major redevelopment and became the centrepiece of the event. The opening and closing ceremonies were staged here, while the athletics competitions took place on the track that surrounded the field.

That Olympic connection remains visible today.

Unlike many modern rugby venues, the stadium retains its athletics configuration, with a running track separating the crowd from the playing surface. While this creates a different atmosphere to the enclosed intensity of venues such as the Principality Stadium, it gives the Olimpico a grandeur and scale few grounds can match.

Every match feels part of a much larger sporting story.

Under the Roman sky

One of the stadium's defining features is its sweeping roof, added as part of a major reconstruction ahead of the 1990 FIFA World Cup. The renovation brought spectators closer to the action while covering much of the seating bowl beneath a modern steel canopy. As daylight fades over Rome, the roof frames views of the surrounding hills and skyline, creating one of the most picturesque settings in international rugby.

Players often speak about the unique feeling of emerging from the tunnel and seeing the bowl illuminated against the Roman evening sky.

Where legends have played

The list of major events staged at the Stadio Olimpico reads like a sporting history book.

The venue hosted the 1960 Olympic Games, the 1990 FIFA World Cup Final, multiple UEFA Champions League finals and countless international fixtures across rugby and football.

  • The stories behind the anthems

For rugby supporters, it has become synonymous with Italy's journey in the Guinness Men's Six Nations. From memorable victories over France and England to the emergence of new generations of Azzurri stars, many of Italian rugby's defining modern moments have taken place here.

The Olimpico is where Italian rugby introduces itself to the world.

The matchday pilgrimage

Every great stadium has its ritual.

On Six Nations weekends, supporters stream through the Foro Italico, passing marble statues, tree-lined avenues and sporting monuments before reaching the ground. The approach combines the grandeur of Rome's sporting district with the energy of a major international event.

Inside, the atmosphere builds steadily.The beat of drums echoes around the bowl, flags flutter from every stand and the singing grows louder as kick-off approaches. When Il Canto degli Italiani rings out before the match, tens of thousands of voices join together beneath the Roman sky.

It is a soundtrack that has become inseparable from Championship rugby.

Behind the scenes

Maintaining the Olimpico requires a balancing act worthy of a Championship-winning fly-half.

Alongside international rugby, the stadium hosts Serie A football, concerts and other major events throughout the year. Grounds staff and stadium crews work continuously to prepare one of Italy's busiest sporting venues.

The operation extends far beyond the pitch, with hospitality suites, media facilities and service areas hidden beneath the stands helping support crowds of more than 70,000 spectators.

Like Rome itself, the stadium never truly stands still.
